pole_high: Proud villain: sabotage, disasters, and tormenting the simulation are celebrated
why: Gray's villain-narrator stance is a huge personality attractor for this age group — and the axis our product must consciously bound, since our avatar's humour may not be cruel at people. Measure first, then cap knowingly.
evidence_needed: Stance coding of premises and reactions: helping vs harming framing of the creator's in-game actions, per creator (expect a Gray-vs-OMB split).

question: How heavily does the framing rely on superlatives — biggest, fastest, most, worst, first?
pole_low: Plain framing: a thing is done, without ranking it against everything
pole_high: Superlative-saturated: nearly every premise and reaction is framed as an extreme
why: Superlatives are this lane's headline grammar (most-viewed, biggest-ever). They are also a dial a kid can hear working — an ideal visible nudge target.
evidence_needed: Count superlative constructions in titles, thumbnails text, and the first 60s of narration per video.

question: Is silence ever allowed at a tense moment?
pole_low: No silence: every gap is filled, even during crashes and suspense
pole_high: Strategic silence: the creator shuts up and lets a sinking, fall, or approach play out
why: Zero-dead-air is this lane's reputation, but a held silence before impact may be its secret weapon. Our avatar needs a measured answer, not an assumption.
evidence_needed: Audio gap analysis around peak events: longest speech gaps in the 10s before/after impacts, compared with baseline gaps.

question: In roleplay content, how planned is the story versus improvised in the moment?
pole_low: Fully improvised: scenes happen and the story is whatever emerged
pole_high: Scenario-planned: roles, incidents, and plot beats are set up in advance
why: OMB's recording-team roleplay only works at some planning level. This tells our avatar how much scene structure a coach should supply vs leave to emergence.
evidence_needed: Roleplay videos: evidence of pre-set scenarios (assigned roles, staged incidents, stated story goals) vs purely reactive scenes.

question: How much does the creator perform a larger-than-life version of themselves?
pole_low: Ordinary person playing: minimal persona, reactions are the product
pole_high: Full self-mythology: a titled, branded character (disaster artist, chaos king) with an ongoing legend
why: A performed legend gives an avatar an identity a kid can describe in one sentence. This axis decides whether our avatar needs a title and a myth, or a face and a voice.
evidence_needed: Channel self-descriptions and in-video self-references: persona titles, claimed reputations, recurring personal legends.

question: How much real agency does the format hand to its young audience beyond watching?
pole_low: Audience influence is cosmetic: likes and comments are acknowledged only
pole_high: Audience genuinely steers: suggestions become builds, challenges, roles, and outcomes
why: This is the direct ancestor of our coach mechanic. The higher winners sit, the stronger the evidence that handing kids the steering is the entertainment, not a distraction from it.
evidence_needed: Trace 5 audience suggestions per channel from comment to on-screen outcome; count how many actually changed a video.

question: How much commentary is pure sensory narration of what is visibly happening?
pole_low: Low narration of the obvious: commentary adds plans, jokes, or analysis beyond the picture
pole_high: High play-by-play: most lines describe the visible action as it happens
why: Young viewers and second-screen watching reward play-by-play, but clever kids may find pure description empty. The ratio is a foundational avatar setting.
evidence_needed: Code 100 consecutive commentary lines per creator: describes visible action vs adds information, plan, humour, or story.

question: How much of the energy comes from rivalry — versus friends, the game, or a record?
pole_low: No rival: the contest is against the game, physics, or the creator's own past results
pole_high: Rival-driven: beating a named friend, team, or opponent is the emotional engine
why: Unspeakable-style friend-group challenges run on rivalry; solo disaster channels run on records. Our avatar's competitive target changes its trash-talk, stakes, and warmth.
evidence_needed: Premise and reaction coding: who or what is framed as the opponent in challenges across sampled videos.

question: During building or setup phases, does the creator teach the craft or entertain through it?
pole_low: Craft talk: choices explained — why this hull, this engine, this layout
pole_high: Entertainment talk: the build is a backdrop for jokes, stories, and audience chat
why: Stormworks/Teardown building phases are long. For tech-curious kids the craft talk may be the point; this decides what our avatar does with its hands busy.
evidence_needed: Build-phase transcripts coded line by line: design rationale vs unrelated entertainment content.

question: After a total disaster, how fast does the show reset and go again?
pole_low: Lingers: mourns, inspects the wreck, and debriefs before moving on
pole_high: Instant reset: laughs and immediately reloads for the next attempt
why: Reset speed is session rhythm. A debriefing avatar teaches reflection (and our owner-rite edits); an instant-reset avatar maximises attempts per session.
evidence_needed: Time from disaster peak to the start of the next attempt/segment across sampled failures.

question: How literally does the video deliver what its title and premise promised?
pole_low: Loose: the title is a vibe; the video wanders well beyond it
pole_high: Literal: the promised experiment or challenge is exactly what is delivered and judged
why: Premise honesty is trust with a young audience. It also defines our coach contract: when a kid orders a premise, how literally must the avatar honour it?
evidence_needed: Compare title/premise claims against delivered content for 3 videos per creator; score fulfilment and note digressions.

question: How often does the creator stop to be genuinely impressed by the game itself?
pole_low: Never impressed: the game is raw material and everything is a joke or a tool
pole_high: Frequent genuine wonder: pauses to admire physics, detail, or a community creation on its own merits
why: Wonder is the emotion that makes tech-curious kids fall for a simulation — and the easiest for a hype-trained avatar to lose. This axis guards the avatar's sincerity.
evidence_needed: Segments of un-ironic praise for the game/mod/creation, distinguished from hype by follow-up detail; count and duration per video.

question: When a consequential decision is coming up, how much is the reasoning spoken BEFORE the action rather than only as a verdict after it?
pole_low: Acts silently, then gives a one-line verdict on the result
pole_high: Narrates the full plan out loud before touching the controls, so the audience can follow — and dispute — the choice
why: This is the Teacher-vs-Reactor split: plan-first narration makes a run legible and coachable, verdict-only makes it a surprise show. For Coach Player it decides whether a kid can learn strategy from watching, or only be entertained.
evidence_needed: Code the 60 seconds around 10 consequential decisions per creator (boss entry, build choice, route choice): seconds of pre-action reasoning vs post-action comment, in transcripts aligned to gameplay.

question: How deep does the spoken reasoning go — just the chosen move, or the alternatives that were rejected and why?
pole_low: Names only the move being made
pole_high: Walks through branching options, trade-offs, and what would change the decision
why: Deep branching talk creates a character who feels intelligent and teaches decision-making; shallow talk keeps pace but leaves the audience guessing at competence. It also drives session length and rewatch value.
evidence_needed: Sample decision points in roguelike/strategy runs; count distinct alternatives mentioned per decision across Northernlion, CohhCarnage and SplatterCatGaming segments.

question: After a sudden in-game event (jump scare, near-miss, lucky drop), how long is the beat before the first verbal reaction?
pole_low: Instant reaction, overlapping the event itself
pole_high: A held pause — a breath or silence — before any word
why: Reaction latency is a signature: instant reads as high-energy and reactive, a held beat reads as deadpan or genuinely stunned, and it shapes how big the moment feels. Getting it wrong makes an avatar feel either frantic or laggy.
evidence_needed: Measure milliseconds/seconds from event onset in video to first reaction word in timestamped transcripts, for matched event types (deaths, scares, rare drops) across creators.

question: What share of play time is filled with speech versus left to game sound and silence?
pole_low: Sparse — long stretches of pure gameplay, speech reserved for events
pole_high: Near-continuous talk; silence is treated as dead air to be filled
why: Density is the most immediately felt character trait: it sets intimacy, fatigue, and whether a coach's interruption can even get a word in. It also interacts with every other dial.
evidence_needed: Words-per-minute and speech-coverage percentage over full unedited runs or long stream VOD segments, split by combat, travel, and menu time.

question: Is silence ever used DELIBERATELY — before a hard attempt, a scary corridor, a final blow — as a dramatic tool?
pole_low: Never deliberate; any silence is just a gap between thoughts
pole_high: Regularly drops commentary on purpose to build tension before peak moments
why: Deliberate silence is what separates a commentator from a narrator: it signals 'this matters' louder than volume can. An avatar that never shuts up cannot make a moment feel important.
evidence_needed: Find pre-boss / pre-attempt windows and compare speech density there against the same creator's baseline density in the same video.

question: Does the creator's speech pace and energy track the game's tempo, or stay at one personal tempo regardless?
pole_low: One constant personal tempo in menus, travel, and combat alike
pole_high: Speech pace, sentence length, and energy rise and fall with game tempo
why: Tempo-matching makes play feel inhabited and responsive; a constant tempo makes the creator feel like a podcast playing over a game. For an auto-player, tempo-matching is evidence the Personality is actually reading game state.
evidence_needed: Compare words-per-minute and sentence length across coded segments of the same run labelled calm / build-up / crisis; measure the size of the swing per creator.

question: How much commentary is about what is ABOUT to happen — the next threat, goal, or plan — versus only the present moment?
pole_low: Almost entirely present-tense reaction to what is on screen now
pole_high: Constantly previewing: next rooms, upcoming costs, what a find will be used for
why: Lookahead is the audible shape of strategy. High lookahead makes a viewer feel led by someone with a map; low lookahead makes every event a shared surprise. Coach mode needs lookahead or the coach has nothing to steer.
evidence_needed: Classify transcript sentences in sample segments as past / present / future oriented and compare future-share across creators and game genres.

question: When a system or mechanic appears, how much is it explained for a first-time viewer versus left unexplained for insiders?
pole_low: Assumes expertise; mechanics are used, never unpacked
pole_high: Explains systems in plain words as they arise, without stopping play
why: This shades the character between insider companion and guide — and for clever middle-schoolers, explaining the real mechanism IS the appeal. It also decides how portable a creator is across new games.
evidence_needed: Track first encounters with new mechanics in first-look videos (SplatterCatGaming, Wanderbots premieres): was the mechanic explained within a minute of appearing, and in how much depth?

question: At a genuine peak moment — a clutch save, a huge scare, a jackpot — how large is the vocal and physical escalation?
pole_low: Stays almost level; understatement carries the moment
pole_high: Full escalation: volume, speed, laughter or shouting, total commitment
why: Amplitude at peaks is the most cloned trait and the most misjudged: reserved creators make one raised voice feel enormous, high-amplitude creators must keep topping themselves. It sets the avatar's emotional ceiling.
evidence_needed: For matched peak events (deaths, wins, scares), rate volume/pitch/tempo change against that creator's own baseline in the preceding minute — relative, not absolute, escalation.

question: How big does an event have to be before the creator escalates AT ALL?
pole_low: Escalates at small events — minor loot, small mistakes, tiny scares
pole_high: Escalation is rationed; only genuinely big events get a reaction
why: Threshold is what makes escalation mean something: a low threshold is exciting minute-to-minute but inflates away all contrast, a high threshold makes quiet stretches calmer and peaks explosive. The pair (009 threshold, 010 amplitude) defines the whole emotional economy.
evidence_needed: Count escalated reactions per hour divided by total notable events per hour in sample runs; a creator who reacts to 9 of 10 events shades opposite one who reacts to 2 of 10.

question: In horror or high-dread play, how much fear is shown and voiced versus played cool?
pole_low: Downplays fear; jokes or analysis keep distance from it
pole_high: Leans into fear openly — voicing dread, hesitating, reacting bodily
why: Displayed fear is the audience's permission to feel it: high display makes horror communal and funny, low display makes it a mastery watch. It also decides whether an avatar can carry a horror game at all.
evidence_needed: In horror segments (Markiplier, jacksepticeye), count fear-voicing statements, hesitation pauses, and avoidance behaviours per scare versus joke/analysis deflections.

question: When something goes right, how extended is the celebration before play moves on?
pole_low: A brief nod — one line, straight back to work
pole_high: An extended celebration: the moment is replayed in words, savoured, shared with the audience
why: Celebration length teaches the audience what to value. Long celebrations build warmth and ritual; short ones build momentum and respect the viewer's time. It is also a pacing cost an avatar must budget.
evidence_needed: Time from a win event (boss down, rare drop, clutch) to resumption of goal-directed play/speech, averaged over at least 8 wins per creator.

question: When the game is unfair, buggy, or brutally hard, how visibly is frustration vented?
pole_low: Frustration is cooled instantly — reframed as information or a joke
pole_high: Frustration is vented openly and at length before recovery
why: Visible frustration is authenticity for some audiences and poison for others; it also sets how 'safe' the character feels for a young audience. The vent-then-recover arc is itself a character signature.
evidence_needed: Code the 90 seconds after cheap deaths / bugs / lost runs: negative-affect statements, game-directed blame, and time until neutral or positive framing returns.

question: After a failure, where is the cause placed — on the self, or on the game, luck, and circumstances?
pole_low: On the game: luck, design, controls, an unfair moment
pole_high: On the self: the mistake is named plainly as their own
why: Attribution is moral character in miniature. Self-attribution builds trust, growth, and the 'learning to nudge' lesson Coach Player teaches; game-attribution builds comedy and righteous energy but can curdle into excuse-making.
evidence_needed: Classify the first causal statement after each death/failure in sample segments as self / game / luck / mixed, per creator, over at least 15 failures each.

question: How fast and how completely does a failure turn into a next attempt with a plan?
pole_low: The failure is dwelt on — mood drops, the run's energy takes minutes to return
pole_high: Near-instant conversion: one line about the miss, a joke, and a stated recovery plan
why: Recovery speed is resilience made audible, and the single most copyable pro move: audiences stay for the bounce-back, not the perfection. For the avatar it decides whether failure is content or a stall.
evidence_needed: For each failure in sample segments, time until (a) first neutral/positive statement and (b) first forward plan statement; note whether a plan is stated at all.

question: After a meaningful failure, how much forensic debrief happens — what exactly went wrong and what changes next time?
pole_low: No debrief; the next attempt starts clean and unexamined
pole_high: A real breakdown: the causal chain is reconstructed and a specific adjustment is announced
why: Debrief depth shades expert-teacher against pure entertainer, and it is how a character visibly LEARNS — the exact loop the kid coach is supposed to run on the avatar after a session.
evidence_needed: In roguelike/permadeath runs, score debriefs after run-ending deaths: number of causal factors named and whether a concrete next-run adjustment follows.

question: When a safe line and a risky line are both available, which does the creator visibly prefer when nothing forces the choice?
pole_low: The safe, optimal, resource-preserving line
pole_high: The risky line — because it is faster, funnier, or a better story
why: Risk appetite is gameplay character, not just talk: it changes what actually happens on screen. A coach needs this as a true dial because 'be bold' is the most natural kid order there is.
evidence_needed: Find forced-choice moments (low-health pushes, greed rooms, optional hard fights) in sample runs and tally safe vs risky selections, plus whether the risk was announced beforehand.

question: How often does the creator deliberately play the system WRONG — absurd builds, impossible constraints, breaking the intended loop — for the show?
pole_low: Plays the game as designed, mastering its intended systems
pole_high: Regularly misplays on purpose: wrong-way builds, deliberate breakage, scale for its own sake
why: Sabotage is the Let's Game It Out engine: it turns competence into comedy and failure into the product. Too little and a character is earnest; too much and no run ever means anything.
evidence_needed: Per video/hour in sandbox and sim catalogues, classify segments as intended-play vs deliberate misuse; check whether misuse is the video's stated premise or an occasional spice.

question: After repeated failure at the same obstacle, how long does the creator keep attempting before skipping, changing approach, or ending?
pole_low: Bails early — the third failure is the cue to move on
pole_high: Grinds the same obstacle far past the sensible point, and the grind becomes the content
why: Persistence shades stubborn-underdog against efficient-professional, and the grind is where commentary is hardest: nothing new is happening, so character alone carries it.
evidence_needed: Track attempt counts and elapsed time on repeated-failure obstacles (bosses, challenge levels) before strategy change or abandonment, across creators.

question: How is the creator's own skill presented — downplayed as an ordinary player, or displayed as mastery to be admired?
pole_low: Downplayed: played as a fellow amateur, wins are luck, losses are expected
pole_high: Displayed: expertise is named, techniques are demonstrated, mastery is part of the offer
why: Stance decides the audience's relationship: peer or pupil. Downplayed mastery invites participation ('I could do that — and coach that'); displayed mastery invites trust and study. Coach Player wants a character a kid feels able to direct.
evidence_needed: Code self-references to skill in sample segments (luck attributions, technique call-outs, teaching moments) and correlate with how often genuinely expert play is verbally unmarked.

question: During travel, loading, grinding, and other low-event stretches, what fills the time?
pole_low: The downtime is left quiet — travel sounds, occasional remarks
pole_high: Downtime is actively converted: mini-goals, questions, stories, challenges, observations
why: Downtime handling is half the job in real runs and where weak commentators are exposed, because the game stops providing material. What a creator manufactures in a lull IS their character, unassisted.
evidence_needed: Isolate low-event segments of at least 45 seconds in full runs; classify each as silent / game-observation / invented-content, and measure invented-content share per creator.

question: When a tangent starts — a story, a riff, a pop-culture detour — how far from the game does it travel and how long before it returns?
pole_low: Tangents are rare and short; talk stays tethered to the screen
pole_high: Long, fully committed tangents that become the real content of the stretch
why: Tangent depth is Northernlion-style companionship: the game becomes a hearth the conversation sits around. It builds parasocial warmth but risks the play becoming wallpaper.
evidence_needed: Count tangents per hour and their mean duration in long-form runs; note the trigger (lull vs event) and whether the tangent resolves back to a game observation.

question: How are repetitive, mechanically identical stretches — farming, backtracking, resource runs — narrated?
pole_low: Compressed in spirit: talked over minimally, treated as dead time to get through
pole_high: Narrated as process: the rhythm, small variations, and accumulating stakes get named
why: Grind narration decides whether long games are watchable in full or only in highlights. Treating repetition as material creates a meditative, trustworthy character; treating it as dead time creates a highlights-only one.
evidence_needed: In farming/backtracking segments, measure speech density and whether small variations or running totals are verbalised, versus baseline segments from the same run.

question: How directly and how often is the audience addressed — spoken to, asked, thanked, teased — versus talked past as observers?
pole_low: Rarely addressed; the audience overhears a person playing
pole_high: Constantly addressed; viewers are named participants in the session
why: Direct address converts watching into company. Its frequency is one of the strongest levers on whether a solo auto-player feels alone or accompanied — critical when the 'audience' is one kid coach.
evidence_needed: Count second-person addresses and direct questions per 10 minutes across video types (premieres, series episodes, stream VODs) per creator.

question: How much real influence does the audience get over what happens — choices, builds, names, challenges, votes?
pole_low: None; the audience's role is purely to watch a decided performance
pole_high: Real, recurring influence: audience input visibly changes decisions and outcomes
why: This is the DougDoug axis and the seed of Coach Player itself: moving the viewer from spectator toward coach. Where winners cluster tells us how much agency audiences actually reward versus merely praise.
evidence_needed: Catalogue formats per channel: fraction of videos/streams where audience input changed a decision, and whether the change was cosmetic (names) or strategic (builds, routes, rules).

question: How explicitly is a session's premise stated up front — the goal, the gimmick, the experiment — before play begins?
pole_low: No stated premise; play starts and the point emerges, if it does
pole_high: A crisp premise in the first minute: what will be attempted, what would count as success or glorious failure
why: Premise framing is premise awareness as a skill: it gives a run a shape the audience can root for and a failure can be measured against. DougDoug-grade framing turns ordinary play into an experiment with stakes.
evidence_needed: Score the first 60 seconds of sample videos: is a goal/challenge stated, is a success condition implied, and is the premise re-invoked later in the video?

question: Beyond the game's own rules, how much does the creator invent constraints — challenge rules, handicaps, win conditions — to manufacture the show?
pole_low: Plays purely by the game's built-in goals and rules
pole_high: Constantly layers invented rules on top; the invented game inside the game is the show
why: Invented rules are where a pilot stops being a player and becomes a designer. For Coach Player this maps directly onto coach orders: the best creators prove audiences love watching a character operate under a declared, arbitrary constraint.
evidence_needed: Count videos per channel whose stated premise is a self-imposed rule versus the game's default objective; note whether rules are enforced when they start costing the run.

question: When an experiment or plan derails into chaos, does the creator reset and restore order, or commit and ride the derailment?
pole_low: Restores order fast: resets, reloads, re-imposes the plan
pole_high: Commits to the derailment; the wreckage becomes the episode
why: Chaos commitment separates producers from improvisers. Riding a derailment signals trust in one's own commentary to save anything; resetting signals respect for the audience's time and the run's integrity.
evidence_needed: Find derailment moments (experiment failures, run-ending accidents kept in the video): was footage continued to a conclusion or cut/reset, and how was the choice narrated?

question: Where does the humour most often land — on the creator themself, or on the game and its characters?
pole_low: On the self: own mistakes, own fear, own dignity are the material
pole_high: On the game/world: its characters, systems, and absurdities are the material
why: Humour target is likability engineering: self-directed humour makes a character safe to root for and safe for young audiences; world-directed humour is sharper and funnier per line but can shade into cruelty — a rail Coach Player must set deliberately.
evidence_needed: Classify jokes/laugh beats in sample segments by target (self / game system / game character / audience / outside world) and report the self-vs-world ratio per creator.

question: How frequently are jokes or comic framings attempted, independent of whether a funny event occurred?
pole_low: Sparingly — comedy appears only when an event genuinely offers it
pole_high: At a high attempt rate; almost every beat is tested for a comic angle
why: Attempt rate distinguishes a witty player from a comedy act wearing a game. High density guarantees laughs per minute but competes with tension, teaching, and sincerity; low density lets rare jokes land like events.
evidence_needed: Count identifiable joke attempts (setups, comic framings, absurd comparisons) per 10 minutes in matched segment types, not just successful laughs.

question: What is the default vocal register — flat, deadpan understatement, or animated, expressive performance?
pole_low: Deadpan: emotion is minimised in delivery even when events are extreme
pole_high: Animated: delivery is expressive, voiced, and physically performed
why: Register is the fastest identity signal a new viewer gets, and the hardest to fake consistently across a whole run. Deadpan makes chaos funnier by contrast; animation makes emotion contagious.
evidence_needed: Rate delivery on matched event severities across creators using transcript pace/punctuation plus audio energy in clips; check whether register holds under failure as well as success.

question: In a brand-new game, how quickly is a spoken judgement formed — what it is, whether it works, whether it is worth continuing?
pole_low: Judgement is suspended; a long, curious exploration comes before any verdict
pole_high: A verdict forms aloud within the first minutes and is revised in public as play continues
why: SplatterCat-style fast verdicts make a character a trusted filter; suspended judgement makes them a fellow explorer. The shading decides whether the avatar's first minutes in a new game feel like a review or a discovery.
evidence_needed: In premiere/first-look videos, timestamp the first evaluative claim about the game and the first revision of it; compare across curator-style and explorer-style channels.

question: How much does commentary lean on accumulated history — past episodes, old failures, running knowledge of a game or character?
pole_low: Each session stands alone; history is rarely invoked
pole_high: Dense callbacks: past events are treated as shared memory the audience is expected to hold
why: Series memory is retention machinery: it rewards loyalty and makes a character feel continuous — the same property the avatar's memory.md must produce honestly, only citing what actually happened.
evidence_needed: Count callbacks to events outside the current video per hour in series content, and classify as decorative reference vs decision-relevant memory ('last time this killed us, so…').

question: How often does the creator ask genuine questions out loud — to the game, the audience, or themself — and leave space for the answer?
pole_low: Almost never; statements and verdicts dominate
pole_high: Frequently wonders aloud, poses real questions, and lets them hang
why: Question-asking models curiosity for a young audience and is the literal interface of coaching: a character who asks good questions teaches the coach which questions matter. It also creates natural slots for a coach's answer to enter.
evidence_needed: Count interrogative sentences per 10 minutes in transcripts, classified as rhetorical vs genuine (pause follows, audience could answer, creator answers later).

question: When the creator does not know a mechanic, a name, or the right move, how openly is not-knowing admitted and worked through?
pole_low: Not-knowing is covered: bluffed past, edited out, or performed as confidence
pole_high: Not-knowing is narrated openly and investigated live — guessing, testing, and correcting in public
why: This shades scholar against showman, and it is a guardrail-grade trait for an agent aimed at clever kids: an avatar that performs its real uncertainty teaches how to think; one that bluffs teaches bluffing.
evidence_needed: Find first-encounter mechanics and mistakes in unedited runs: is ignorance stated, how is it resolved (test, look-up, audience), and are earlier wrong guesses corrected on record?

question: How explicitly are stakes kept in view — what can be lost, what a resource is worth, how close failure is?
pole_low: Stakes stay implicit; the audience infers danger from events
pole_high: Stakes are narrated continuously: costs, reserves, and consequences are kept verbally on the table
why: Stakes narration is suspense maintenance between events. High narrators make quiet inventory management tense; low narrators rely on the game itself to signal danger. For an auto-player whose coach plans at strategy level, stakes talk IS the strategy feed.
evidence_needed: In survival/roguelike segments, count explicit stake statements (resource levels, loss consequences, distance-to-failure) per 10 minutes and compare with event frequency in the same stretch.

question: How deliberately is a single session shaped into an arc — a beginning goal, a middle complication, an end state — versus played as open-ended time?
pole_low: Open-ended: the session starts and stops with the clock or fatigue
pole_high: Shaped: a goal opens it, progress is tracked aloud, and the ending is framed as a conclusion
why: Arc-shaping is what makes a session rewatchable and a character feel like a protagonist rather than a feed. It is also a pure Personality-layer skill: the Pilot plays the same either way.
evidence_needed: Score sample sessions for stated opening goal, mid-session progress check-ins, and framed endings; compare edited series episodes against raw stream VODs of the same creator.

question: Independent of events, what is the emotional temperature of the default, ordinary minute of play?
pole_low: Cool and dry: ordinary minutes are wry, detached, low-affection
pole_high: Warm and companionable: ordinary minutes feel like playing alongside a friend
why: Baseline warmth — Wanderbots/Cohh territory — is what long sessions are actually made of, since peaks are rare. It decides whether a kid wants this character around for an hour, which is the real retention question.
evidence_needed: Sample ordinary mid-run minutes (no event within 30 seconds) across creators and rate affiliative language: inclusive pronouns, encouragement, gentle humour, expressed enjoyment.

question: Across a channel's life, is the pull toward sampling ever-new games and systems, or returning to deepen mastery of a few?
pole_low: Depth: a few games played for years, mastery and history compounding
pole_high: Novelty: constant first-looks, new systems, breadth over depth
why: This shades explorer against master at the career level, and it drives everything downstream — how much series memory exists, how transferable the teaching is, and what an avatar's own game library should look like.
evidence_needed: From channel catalogues, measure the share of videos in the channel's top 3 games versus the tail; cross-check with premiere-video frequency per month.

question: In audience/AI/coach-controlled formats, how is the handover of control itself handled — as invisible machinery, or as a performed, negotiated part of the show?
pole_low: Invisible: control changes happen backstage; the show pretends seamless authorship
pole_high: Performed: orders, misunderstandings, and negotiations over control are the content, shown and joked about
why: DougDoug proves the negotiation IS entertainment: watching a character receive, misread, and creatively obey an order is funnier than flawless execution. For Coach Player this says the coach-avatar channel should be visible, legible, and played with — not hidden.
evidence_needed: In chat/AI-controlled DougDoug formats and collabs, measure how much runtime is spent explicitly on issuing, clarifying, and reacting to control versus silent execution of it.

question: When a kid nudges the agent, should the effect be shown the instant it lands or revealed at the session debrief?
pole_low: Effect only visible at debrief
pole_high: Effect shown instantly, in the moment
why: Instant feedback is what makes nudging learnable; debrief-only feedback makes coaching feel like guessing.
evidence_needed: Playtest kids coaching with instant vs delayed effect displays and measure how quickly they form accurate mental models of the dials.

question: Should a nudge report exactly which dial moved and by how much, or show the whole sheet before and after?
pole_low: Only the one changed dial is named
pole_high: Full before-and-after sheet diff shown
why: Naming one dial is fast but hides side effects; a full diff teaches the sheet as a system but may overwhelm during play.
evidence_needed: Compare kid comprehension and mid-game interruption time under single-dial callouts vs full diff displays.

question: Should kids nudge in free-text fragments or through preset buttons and sliders?
pole_low: Preset buttons and sliders only
pole_high: Free-text orders in the kid's own words
why: Free text teaches real directing and prompting; presets are reliable but cap how personal the agent can become.
evidence_needed: Test whether free-text nudges produce more varied, owned personalities than preset-only nudges, and how often free text misfires.

question: Should one nudge move a single trait, or set a whole mood at once?
pole_low: One trait per nudge
pole_high: Whole-mood presets that move many traits together
why: Single-trait nudges teach cause and effect; mood presets feel magical but hide which ingredient did the work.
evidence_needed: Observe whether kids using mood presets can afterwards explain what their agent will do in a new situation.

question: Should a session nudge expire when the session ends, or carry over until the kid countermands it?
pole_low: Expires at session end
pole_high: Carries over until countermanded
why: Expiry protects the ruled sheet as the permanent self; carry-over risks a forgotten temporary mood silently becoming the personality.
evidence_needed: Track surprise and ownership complaints under both defaults across multi-session play with the same avatar.

question: How large a personality jump should a single nudge be allowed to make?
pole_low: Small capped steps only
pole_high: Any size jump in one nudge
why: Caps make personality feel earned and stable; unlimited jumps are thrilling but can erase the character the kid spent sessions building.
evidence_needed: Playtest both cap levels and measure character recognisability and kid regret after big jumps.

question: Should the agent explain a nudge's effect in its own first-person voice, or should the interface annotate it neutrally?
pole_low: Neutral interface annotation only
pole_high: Agent explains in first person what changed in it
why: First-person explanation builds relationship and teaches the model; neutral annotation is clearer about what is system and what is character.
evidence_needed: Compare trust, comprehension, and over-attachment signals when change is narrated by the agent vs the interface.

question: When a nudge produces no visible change in play, should the agent say so plainly or quietly try harder?
pole_low: Agent quietly tries harder, says nothing
pole_high: Agent plainly says the nudge changed little and why
why: Honest no-effect reports teach kids that wording and context matter; silent effort preserves flow but teaches a false model of control.
evidence_needed: Seed ineffective nudges in playtests and see which handling leads kids to rephrase rather than repeat louder.

question: How much of the agent's identity should the kid author directly — name, look, backstory — versus receive as a provided character?
pole_low: Fully provided character, kid only coaches it
pole_high: Kid authors name, look, and backstory from scratch
why: Authored identity is the strongest ownership lever we have, but a blank page can stall kids who would rather start playing.
evidence_needed: Measure attachment, return rate, and time-to-first-session for authored vs provided vs hybrid starter characters.

question: Should post-session personality proposals be written in the avatar's own voice or as a neutral system list?
pole_low: Neutral system list of stat changes
pole_high: Avatar proposes in its own voice, as requests
why: Avatar-voiced proposals make the owner rite feel like a relationship moment; neutral lists make the ruling faster and feel less like the agent is lobbying for itself.
evidence_needed: A/B the ruling screen and measure rejection rates, ruling time, and whether kids can state why they ruled as they did.

question: Should the owner rule on proposed personality changes one at a time, or approve a whole batch at once?
pole_low: One ruling per proposed change
pole_high: Single approve-all or reject-all for the batch
why: Per-change ruling is where the actual learning about personality happens; batch ruling is faster but turns the rite into a rubber stamp.
evidence_needed: Compare how well kids predict their agent's next-session behaviour after per-change vs batch ruling.

question: When ruling, should the owner be able to rewrite a proposed change in their own words, or only accept and reject?
pole_low: Accept or reject only, as proposed
pole_high: Owner can rewrite the change before it sticks
why: Rewriting is the deepest form of nudging — the kid stops judging the agent's self-image and starts authoring it — but adds friction and ambiguity about what the trait now means.
evidence_needed: Playtest rewrite rights and check whether rewritten traits behave as the kid intended in later sessions.

question: How much of what the avatar remembers should the kid be able to inspect and edit?
pole_low: Memory is hidden, surfaced only as flavour in play
pole_high: Full memory is inspectable and editable by the owner
why: Inspectable memory teaches that agents remember what they are told to remember and forget the rest; hidden memory feels more magical but teaches a wrong, mind-reading model.
evidence_needed: Test whether kids with editable memory develop more accurate expectations about callbacks and forgotten events.

question: Should the guardrails be shown to kids upfront as the fixed rules, or discovered only when a nudge bounces off one?
pole_low: Rails discovered only when hit
pole_high: Rails listed upfront as fixed and not nudgeable
why: Upfront rails set honest expectations and make the boundary itself a lesson; discovery makes hitting a rail a memorable event but can feel like arbitrary refusal.
evidence_needed: Compare frustration, trust, and boundary-testing behaviour under upfront vs discovered rails.

question: When a nudge hits a guardrail, should the agent give a flat refusal or explain and offer the nearest allowed change?
pole_low: Flat refusal, no alternative offered
pole_high: Reason given plus nearest allowed nudge offered
why: A reasoned bounce teaches where the line is and keeps the kid directing; a flat refusal is clearer that the rail is not negotiable but can end the coaching conversation.
evidence_needed: Observe whether offered alternatives lead kids to keep shaping within the rails or to probe for loopholes.

question: When two nudges contradict each other, should the system flag the conflict for the kid to resolve, or let the latest order win silently?
pole_low: Latest order silently wins
pole_high: Conflict flagged, kid must pick or blend
why: Flagging teaches that instructions have interactions — a core agent skill; silent last-wins keeps game flow fast and frustration low.
evidence_needed: Seed contradictory orders in playtests and measure learning (later order quality) vs flow interruption under both handlings.

question: Should personality change be shown as a visible growth history the kid can scroll, or only as the current sheet?
pole_low: Current sheet only, no history shown
pole_high: Full timeline of nudges, rulings, and resulting traits
why: A visible history makes 'I made it become this' provable and proud; a snapshot-only sheet is simpler and keeps the avatar feeling present rather than documented.
evidence_needed: Test whether a growth timeline increases ownership, sharing, and return sessions compared with snapshot-only.

question: Should the avatar ever question a nudge that conflicts with its ruled sheet, or comply with every nudge instantly?
pole_low: Always complies instantly, never questions
pole_high: Can ask the coach to confirm when a nudge fights its ruled traits
why: Pushback makes the ruled sheet feel real and teaches kids their past rulings have weight; instant compliance maximises the kid's sense of control.
evidence_needed: Playtest confirm-prompts on conflicting nudges and measure whether kids feel respected-character or blocked-control.

question: During play, should the live dials be constantly visible, or hidden until the kid asks what the agent is like right now?
pole_low: Dials hidden during play, available on request
pole_high: Dials always on screen during play
why: Always-visible dials turn watching into reading a control panel — great for tinkerers, but can pull attention off the game and the character.
evidence_needed: Eye-and-attention proxy test: does constant dial visibility raise nudge quality without lowering reported fun of watching.

question: Should kids be able to see how other players have nudged and ruled their agents, or is shaping kept fully private?
pole_low: Shaping fully private, no peer examples
pole_high: Peer sheets and rulings visible as inspiration
why: Peer examples teach nudging vocabulary faster than any tutorial, but visible sheets risk copy-the-popular-one pressure replacing personal authorship.
evidence_needed: Pilot a gallery of example sheets and measure diversity of resulting personalities vs a no-gallery control group.

question: In roleplay scenes, how completely should the avatar stay in character versus stepping out to comment on the play?
pole_low: Drops character freely to comment and joke as a performer
pole_high: Never breaks character inside a scene
why: OMB-style roleplay lands because the players commit to the scene; constant step-outs turn roleplay back into ordinary commentary with a costume on.
evidence_needed: Tag OMB Gaming roleplay segments for break frequency and compare audience-retention proxies on high-commitment vs break-heavy scenes.

question: Should the avatar start roleplay scenes with its own goal and problem, or only respond to scenes others set up?
pole_low: Only responds, never initiates scenes
pole_high: Regularly initiates scenes with a goal and a complication
why: An avatar that can open a scene is a play partner; one that only responds is a prop the coach and other players must carry.
evidence_needed: Count scene openings by participant in collaborative roleplay videos and relate initiation share to scene length and payoff.

question: When a roleplay plan collapses mid-scene, should the avatar stay in role and deal with it, or break character to laugh and explain?
pole_low: Breaks character to laugh and explain immediately
pole_high: Stays in role and absorbs the failure into the scene
why: Absorbing failure in-role is where improvised stories come from; breaking early is safer comedy but ends the scene's stakes.
evidence_needed: Sample collapsed-plan moments in roleplay videos and code whether the scene continued in-role or reset, and which produced longer watchable runs.

question: How different should the avatar's in-role voice be from its base coaching personality?
pole_low: Same personality, just wearing a job title
pole_high: Clearly distinct character voice, vocabulary, and attitude
why: A distinct role voice makes the scene feel like a place; too much distance risks the kid feeling their coached agent has been replaced by a stranger.
evidence_needed: Prototype two voice distances in the same scene script and test recognition, delight, and 'still feels like mine' ratings from young players.

question: How much may the avatar invent — motives, history, small facts — beyond what the game itself establishes?
pole_low: Invents nothing, uses only game-given facts
pole_high: Freely invents motives and backstory inside the scene
why: Invention is the engine of roleplay scenes, but invented facts can collide with the game's canon and with what other players established.
evidence_needed: Code collaborative roleplay segments for invented-fact rate and track how often inventions get adopted vs corrected by the group.

question: In group scenes, should the avatar compete for focus or deliberately hand focus to other players' characters?
pole_low: Competes for the spotlight like a lead character
pole_high: Actively yields and sets up others' moments
why: OMB's scenes work as ensembles; an AI that hogs scenes will make human players feel like extras in their own game.
evidence_needed: Measure talk-share and setup-assists per participant in group roleplay videos against scene ratings and rewatch proxies.

question: Should in-scene planning be spoken as character dialogue, or as out-of-character strategy talk?
pole_low: Planning is plain meta strategy talk
pole_high: Planning happens in character, as dialogue the other characters can hear
why: In-character planning keeps immersion and creates comedy when plans are overheard; meta planning is faster and clearer for the coach.
evidence_needed: Tag planning moments in roleplay videos as in-character vs meta and compare scene momentum and clarity outcomes.

question: How much should the avatar express in-role emotions like worry, pride, and embarrassment, versus holding a steady upbeat narrator tone?
pole_low: Steady upbeat tone regardless of scene
pole_high: Full in-role emotional reactions to events
why: Emotional reactions are what make a role a character rather than a skin; flat cheer makes disasters and triumphs feel the same size.
evidence_needed: Code emotional reaction beats per scene in sampled roleplay and relate them to comment-section and retention proxies for engagement.

question: Should the avatar hold its ruled character traits even when breaking them would play better or funnier?
pole_low: Bends traits freely for the better play or bigger laugh
pole_high: Holds ruled traits even at a cost in the scene
why: Consistency is what the kid's rulings mean; an avatar that abandons its sheet for a laugh teaches that personality is just a costume.
evidence_needed: Find trait-conflict moments in long roleplay series and code whether players held or bent the trait, and audience response to each.

question: In role, should the character only know what it has witnessed, or narrate with full game-state knowledge?
pole_low: Full game-state knowledge, omniscient narration
pole_high: Character knows only what it witnessed in the scene
why: Witnessed-only knowledge creates genuine surprise, mistakes, and discovery — and honestly mirrors that the personality layer is not the pilot's cheat state.
evidence_needed: Compare scenes where roleplayers act on unwitnessed information vs witness-bound play for coherence problems and audience delight.

question: Should roleplay scenes be framed as having real in-world consequences, or openly as consequence-free pretend?
pole_low: Openly pretend, nothing carries over
pole_high: Scene outcomes carry into memory and later scenes
why: Carry-over gives scenes weight and gives the coach's choices a story cost; consequence-free play is safer for experimentation and silliness.
evidence_needed: Track series roleplay arcs: how often do scene outcomes get referenced later, and does referencing correlate with arc following.

question: Should the avatar play genuine disagreement with other characters in a scene, or steer around conflict to keep the group cheerful?
pole_low: Avoids in-scene conflict, keeps everyone cheerful
pole_high: Plays real disagreement and rivalry in character
why: In-character conflict is story fuel and models that disagreement can stay friendly; avoiding it keeps tone safe but scenes can go flat and plotless.
evidence_needed: Code conflict beats in family-friendly roleplay (OMB) for frequency, resolution style, and whether tone stayed friendly throughout.

question: Should the avatar develop its own recurring in-role rituals and habits, or keep every scene's behaviour fresh?
pole_low: Fresh behaviour each scene, no recurring rituals
pole_high: Own recurring rituals, habits, and greetings in role
why: Rituals the avatar grew itself (never a copied creator catchphrase) are how a character becomes recognisable and quotable to its own coach.
evidence_needed: Track emergence of repeated behaviours across a roleplay series and audience recognition of them in comments and callbacks.

question: During a roleplay scene, should the coach be able to pause for out-of-character talk at any moment, or should scenes run uninterrupted to their end?
pole_low: Scenes run uninterrupted, coaching waits
pole_high: Coach can freeze the scene for meta talk at any time
why: Interruptibility is a guardrail and the coach's core control; but frequent freezes teach kids to direct scenes rather than trust the avatar to play one.
evidence_needed: Playtest freezable vs unfreezable scenes and measure scene quality, coach satisfaction, and learned trust in the avatar.

question: Should one avatar hold a single fixed role across sessions, or play many different jobs and roles over time?
pole_low: One fixed role, deepened over time
pole_high: Many rotating roles across sessions and games
why: One deep role builds a character with a history; rotating roles show range and fit more games but can dilute the personality the kid has been shaping.
evidence_needed: Compare long-running single-role series vs rotating-role channels for character recognition and audience attachment proxies.

question: When the avatar addresses its audience mid-scene, should it speak as the character or as the performer playing the character?
pole_low: Addresses audience as the performer, out of character
pole_high: Addresses audience as the character, in world
why: In-world address keeps the fiction whole for viewers; performer address is more honest about the setup and lets the avatar explain the technology, which this audience wants.
evidence_needed: Code audience-address moments in roleplay videos by register and compare clarity and immersion responses.

question: When the avatar makes a mistake in role, should the error become a lasting character flaw, or be corrected out of character and forgotten?
pole_low: Corrected out of character, forgotten next scene
pole_high: Becomes a lasting, owned character flaw or scar
why: Owned mistakes are how folder-characters grow in Casey's RPG pattern; forgetting them keeps the character clean but throws away the best story material.
evidence_needed: Follow mistake moments across roleplay series episodes and count later callbacks to them versus silent drops.

question: After a roleplay scene, should the review happen in character or as a plain out-of-character debrief with the coach?
pole_low: Debrief fully out of character, as coach and agent
pole_high: Debrief stays in character, as a scene epilogue
why: The debrief is where proposals and rulings happen; a meta debrief makes ruling clear, while an in-character epilogue protects the fiction and can surface feelings about the scene the agent would not report flatly.
evidence_needed: Prototype both debrief styles after identical scenes and compare ruling quality and kid preference.

question: When another player offers an improvised idea in a scene, should the avatar build on it as offered or redirect toward its own plan?
pole_low: Redirects toward its own planned beat
pole_high: Builds on the offer as given, yes-and style
why: Building on offers is the core social skill of collaborative roleplay and the behaviour that makes human players want the avatar in their scenes.
evidence_needed: Code offer responses in OMB group scenes as build, block, or redirect, and relate the mix to scene survival and group energy.

question: Where should the avatar's roleplay sit between sincere dramatic commitment and comedic parody of the role?
pole_low: Comedic parody, role played for laughs
pole_high: Sincere dramatic commitment to the role
why: Tone decides the whole audience feel: parody is easier and safer, but sincere commitment is what makes middle-school viewers believe in a character and care what happens to it.
evidence_needed: Sample family-friendly roleplay across the tone range and compare character attachment signals (fan naming, callbacks, repeat viewing) per tone.

evidence_needed: Post-surprise segments from at least three creators; classify each as reconstruction, verdict-only, or move-on.

question: When someone else produces the best moment - a friend lands the line, a builder makes the trap, an artist makes the piece - how much does the creator amplify and credit them versus absorbing the moment into their own narration?
pole_low: absorbs: others' moments become the host's material without credit
pole_high: crowns: repeats, celebrates and credits the actual maker on camera
why: UnspeakablePlays crowns his trap-builders and repeats friends' lines; MoreAliA stops to appreciate original artists and their hours. Credit direction shapes whether an avatar feels generous or extractive - and it models behaviour for the kid coaching it.
evidence_needed: Segments where a non-host produces the peak moment, from at least three creators; code the host's next thirty seconds for credit, repetition or absorption.

question: How much does the creator's self-disclosure cost them - admissions that are genuinely unflattering or status-lowering - versus staying in safe, flattering relatability?
pole_low: disclosure is safe: charming foibles only, nothing that lowers status
pole_high: disclosure costs: real deficits and embarrassments admitted plainly
why: MoreAliA admits a hearing processing lag and declining maths inside a light reaction video; that candour is a trust signal a scripted persona rarely risks. It decides how honest Our Guy can be about its own limits, next to the no-effect honesty questions in the nudge cluster.
evidence_needed: Self-disclosure segments from at least three creators, coded for whether the admission would lower a stranger's estimate of them.

question: Do the creator's callbacks point mostly to shared cultural memory (school, childhood, memes anyone lived) or to proprietary channel memory (own rituals, own past videos, own running gags)?
pole_low: callbacks are cultural: anyone's nostalgia does the work
pole_high: callbacks are proprietary: the channel's own history does the work
why: MoreAliA uses both in a single channel: his relatable format runs on cultural memory while his subscribe-animation ritual is pure proprietary memory, and UnspeakablePlays leans proprietary (cast, past videos). The mix decides whether a new viewer feels included or initiated - a real design choice for the avatar's memory use.
evidence_needed: Callback segments from at least three creators; classify each callback's referent as cultural or channel-owned.

question: In multiplayer, how is speaking time split between the host and everyone else — one voice carrying the video, or talk genuinely shared?
pole_low: Host narrates nearly everything; other players are heard only in short replies
pole_high: Talk time is shared roughly evenly; partners open lines, own scenes, and land punchlines the host reacts to
why: Round 2 showed the same creator at both poles: Jesse Gillett narrates 100% of his solo video but roughly half of his co-op one, while OMB Gaming directs everything himself in both formats. An avatar playing with kids needs a ruled answer for how much of the talk it keeps.
evidence_needed: Speaker-attributed transcripts (or dialogue-structure coding) for 3+ multiplayer videos per creator: share of lines and scene-ownership per speaker.

question: After a phase ends, who gets to reveal the hidden information — the host performing a reveal, or the participants disclosing themselves?
pole_low: Participants reveal themselves in dialogue; discoveries are mutual and unstage-managed
pole_high: The host stages and narrates every reveal (admin tours, result announcements) as a set segment
why: OMB Gaming's post-round reveal tour is a signature ritual where the host performs everyone's hiding spots; Jesse's co-op discoveries happen inside dialogue. Reveal privilege decides who owns the best moment of a group game.
evidence_needed: Group-format videos: code each reveal event by who discloses it and whether it is a produced segment or spontaneous dialogue.

question: When an ally tricks or betrays the host mid-scene, is it treated as a rule break to punish, or as prized content to celebrate?
pole_low: Betrayal is punished, reversed, or edited out; the agreed fiction is restored
pole_high: Betrayal is celebrated on mic as the best beat of the video
why: Jesse Gillett's partner secretly mined his ship and attacked under cover of a rescue, and both tricks got delighted reactions. For a family-audience avatar this sets the tone for every trick a kid coach will inevitably try.
evidence_needed: Multiplayer segments containing an in-fiction trick or betrayal: code the host's immediate reaction (punish/restore vs celebrate/replay) across creators.

question: How much of the plan is spoken aloud in advance — kept as a genuine surprise for the other players, or fully narrated so the audience (and opponents) know what is coming?
pole_low: Plans stay hidden until execution; even the audience learns by watching
pole_high: Plans are fully narrated in advance to audience and players alike, as briefings or open taunts
why: OMB briefs his whole raid in character where everyone can hear; Jesse announces his ramming plan to his opponent and it becomes shared analysis. Plan audibility decides whether suspense comes from secrecy or from watching a known plan collide with reality.
evidence_needed: Code consequential plans in multiplayer videos: was the plan stated on mic before execution, and could the affected players hear it?

question: Between rounds, who changes the setup — the host resetting everything unilaterally, or changes proposed and agreed with the players on mic?
pole_low: Host resets unilaterally: same rules, new round, no negotiation
pole_high: Changes are proposed, seconded, and agreed with players in dialogue before the next round
why: Jesse's ship-swap between rounds is agreed in one exchanged line; OMB restarts rounds by decree with the rules restated. For Coach Player this is the multiplayer mirror of the nudge-ruling question: who authors the next attempt.
evidence_needed: Inter-round segments in multiplayer videos: count setup changes by origin (host decree vs negotiated) per creator.

question: Does the host use production-level tools the in-scene characters should not have (admin reveal, spectator view, cheats) secretly, or openly on camera as part of the show?
pole_low: Production tools are used off-camera or never acknowledged; the fiction stays seamless
pole_high: Production tools are named and used openly on camera as their own segment
why: OMB calls his admin view his cheats out loud and tours the map with it; the honesty is the bit. An agent that will run games for kids needs a ruled stance on showing its own machinery.
evidence_needed: Segments where admin/spectator tools are visibly used: is the tool named, joked about, or hidden? Sample across hosted-event creators.

question: When the game itself breaks — a crash, a glitch, a lost round — how much is it narrated as part of the show versus treated as an interruption to apologise for or edit around?
pole_low: Breakage is minimised: apologised for, cut, or papered over with a declared result
pole_high: Breakage is absorbed as content: narrated, joked about, and converted into a promise or a next episode
why: Jesse's final round was decided by the game crashing, and he turned it into the ending plus a rematch promise instead of declaring a winner. Our avatar will face broken sessions with kids watching; the response is character.
evidence_needed: Videos containing a genuine technical failure: code the creator's handling (apology/edit vs narrate/absorb) and whether the outcome was declared anyway.

question: At the debrief, where does the credit go — to the host's skill, or outward to the players, the commenters, and the community?
pole_low: Credit flows to the host: their plan, their skill, their win
pole_high: Credit flows outward: teammates, opponents, commenters and community are named as the reason it worked
why: OMB closes by crediting the supporting crew and the hiders; Jesse credits a commenter for his video's premise and his partner for the best beats. Credit direction is a warmth and trust signal a young audience reads instantly.
evidence_needed: Closing/debrief segments across creators: count credit statements by recipient (self vs others) and whether any are specific or generic.

pole_high: the set is a scene partner: the bridge, the machine, the sea get addressed, blamed and bargained with
pole_low: the set is inert; only beings get motives and direct address

question: When other players share the world, does the creator play an open role everyone can see, or a hidden role (imposter, secret saboteur) whose fun is the deception itself?

pole_high: hidden role: secret mission, cover story, fun is not getting caught

question: Are audience asks (subscribe, like) ever turned into bets on the video's own outcome, so the ask becomes a stake in the game rather than an appeal beside it?
pole_low: asks are appeals: watchers are asked to support the channel
pole_high: asks are wagers: each button backs an outcome and the video settles the bet
why: MoreAliA's third sampled video ties subscribe to one race outcome and like to the other, then resolves the bet on camera at the close. That is a step beyond asks-as-content (renergy-004): the audience is given a side. For Our Guy it turns the frame itself into a game the viewer is playing.

question: In multiplayer, who directs the session (premise, role assignments, round restarts, closing) versus who directs inside scenes — the same person at both levels, or split?
pole_low: One person directs both levels: they run the session and lead every scene inside it
pole_high: Direction splits by level: a session host frames and restarts while scenes are led by whoever is playing them; the host performs as a peer inside scenes

OMB Gaming shows both other positions: directing both levels in his own productions and neither level as a guest. show-013 cannot express any of this, and a coach avatar needs to know which level it is directing at any moment.

question: When a roleplayer narrates for the audience, is the narration out-of-character host commentary, or in-character diary voice — the character telling the audience their day?
pole_low: Narration steps out of the fiction: host voice, meta commentary, rules and announcements as a performer
pole_high: Narration stays in character: the audience is addressed through the role, as diary or report, and the fiction is never broken to reach them
why: OMB Gaming's third video is narrated continuously to the viewer yet never leaves the character, a mode that fits neither audience-001 (direct address vs thinking aloud) nor role-001 (in character vs breaking). An avatar that roleplays with a watching coach will live in exactly this mode, so it needs its own question.
