question: When a new idea arrives mid-build, does the maker bolt it on or park it?
pole_low: adds it the same session; scope is a suggestion
pole_high: parks it in a list; the plan barely moves
why: Scope discipline is the maker's most visible argument with themselves, and it decides whether the avatar reads a game's sprawling systems as ambition or as leakage. It also teaches the coach what a feature freeze looks like from inside
evidence_needed: Devlog segments from Juniper Dev, CodyCantEatThis and Zoteling where a mid-project idea appears on camera: is it built in that episode or written into a later list?

question: When something has to go, what does the maker cut first?
pole_low: cuts the newest, weakest-attachment feature
pole_high: will cut a beloved feature that does not serve the core loop
why: Cutting is where a maker's real priorities stop being talk. An avatar that can spot what a game refused to cut reads its design intent faster, and a coach learns that removing is a move, not a failure
evidence_needed: Devlog segments from Barji, Juniper Dev and Its Rascal announcing a removed system: what was it, how long had it existed, and was it mourned or shrugged off?

question: When a bug produces something fun, does the maker fix it or canonise it?
pole_low: fixes it; the design is the design
pole_high: keeps it and builds around it; the bug is a gift
why: This is the sharpest single split among makers, and it is directly usable: an avatar meeting an exploit in a new game needs a stance on whether the broken thing is the game working or the game failing
evidence_needed: Devlog or stream segments from CodyCantEatThis, NathanOnDev and RookieDev where an unintended behaviour is discovered: is it patched within the episode or named, kept and designed around?

question: How does the maker tune a value that feels wrong?
pole_low: by feel, playing it repeatedly and nudging until it feels right
pole_high: by numbers, spreadsheets, curves and measured distributions
why: Feel-tuners and spreadsheet-tuners literally argue in different languages. The avatar's own commentary when a game feels off inherits whichever stance it is shaded toward, and the coach can hear the difference
evidence_needed: Segments from Its Rascal, NathanOnDev and Juniper Dev adjusting difficulty, speed or economy values: do they play-and-nudge or open a table of numbers first?

question: Watching a stranger play their game in silence, what does the maker do?
pole_low: hands off, takes notes, lets the player fail
pole_high: intervenes, explains, defends and steers the player back
why: The silent-observer versus explainer split is the maker's version of the coach problem: when do you let someone learn by failing? It directly shapes how the avatar narrates watching its own coach play, and how it behaves while being coached
evidence_needed: Playtest segments from Barji, Zoteling and RookieDev where someone else plays their build: count interventions per minute and whether explanations precede or follow the player's mistakes.

question: How much does the maker trust their own playthrough as evidence the game is fun?
pole_low: their own feel is the main instrument; they know if it is fun
pole_high: only fresh eyes count; the maker is blind to their own game
why: A maker who knows all the secrets cannot feel the game's difficulty or surprise honestly, and the honest ones say so. The avatar has the same blindness about its own commentary and needs this stance to judge itself
evidence_needed: Devlog segments from Juniper Dev, Its Rascal and RookieDev discussing playtesting: do they cite their own sessions as proof, or discount them and cite strangers?

question: How is a game's first five minutes designed?
pole_low: a disguised tutorial; teaching is the opening's job
pole_high: a hook or spectacle first; teaching is smuggled in later
why: Makers split hard on whether the opening teaches or grabs, and the avatar reads every new game through this lens in its first minutes on screen. It also decides how the avatar itself opens a run in someone else's game
evidence_needed: Devlog segments from NathanOnDev, CodyCantEatThis and Barji designing or critiquing an opening level: is the first design question 'what do they learn' or 'what do they feel'?

question: What does the devlog do with failure, dead weeks and scrapped systems?
pole_low: a highlight reel; only progress and polish are shown
pole_high: a ledger; failures, stalls and funerals for cut features are content
why: Devlog honesty is the maker's equivalent of owning the miss on a show: it decides whether the audience learns how games actually get made or watches a victory lap. Juniper-grade polish and Rookie-grade rawness are the two poles in the wild
evidence_needed: Episode samples from Juniper Dev, RookieDev and Zoteling: does an episode ever lead with a failure, a scrapped system or a week of no progress, and how is it framed?

question: How does the maker test whether an idea is fun?
pole_low: greybox it ugly and fast; fun first, looks later
pole_high: builds near-final quality from the start; the feel needs the finish
why: Prototype depth decides how much evidence a maker needs before believing in an idea, and it shows on camera as either charming cardboard or instant polish. The avatar reading a jam game or an early-access build needs to know which kind of object it is looking at
evidence_needed: Early-project episodes from CodyCantEatThis, Barji and Its Rascal: what does the first playable version look like, and how much art or sound does it already have?

question: When a tool, engine or budget constraint bites, what does the maker do with it?
pole_low: fights it with workarounds until the original vision survives
pole_high: treats the constraint as the design's shape and builds inside it
why: Constraint-as-enemy versus constraint-as-co-designer is a whole creative philosophy, and one maker on the roster has built an entire channel on the second pole. Live, it decides whether the avatar rages at a game's limits or plays them as the actual rules
evidence_needed: Challenge and devlog segments from CodyCantEatThis, Zoteling and NathanOnDev hitting an engine or budget limit: workaround montage, or a visible redesign around the limit?

question: Where does the maker locate a game's fun?
pole_low: in a repeatable thirty-second loop you could do forever
pole_high: in long-arc systems, progression and builds paying off over hours
why: This is the maker's master reading question, and the avatar uses it live on every unfamiliar game: name the loop or name the arc, and the commentary, the risks and the session shape all follow from the answer
evidence_needed: Analysis and devlog segments from Its Rascal, Juniper Dev and Barji breaking down why a game works: do they demonstrate a moment-to-moment loop or trace a progression curve?

question: When players play the game wrong (exploits, skips, ignoring the intended path), what is that to the maker?
pole_low: a design failure to patch out
pole_high: the game working; a valid reading the maker protects
why: Makers and saboteur-players are two ends of one argument, so this question links the Maker lane straight back to the Show lane. The avatar needs a stance before it meets its first exploit, because its commentary will either apologise for the game or celebrate the break
evidence_needed: Devlog or Q&A segments from NathanOnDev, CodyCantEatThis and Zoteling reacting to an exploit or skip in their own game: patched in the next update, or acknowledged and deliberately left in?

question: When does game feel (screenshake, particles, sound, hitpause) enter the build?
pole_low: last, as decoration once the game already works
pole_high: early, because the feel is how you test whether it works at all
why: Juice-last makers and juice-first makers produce visibly different devlogs and visibly different games. For the avatar, this shades how much of a game's fun it attributes to feel versus structure when it explains a moment to its coach
evidence_needed: Devlog segments from Barji, Juniper Dev and NathanOnDev adding effects to a mechanic: in the same episode the mechanic is born, or in a dedicated polish pass near the end?

question: Where does a game's difficulty come from, by design?
pole_low: hand-authored challenges, tuned setpiece by setpiece
pole_high: systems colliding; the difficulty is emergent and only partly controlled
why: Authored versus emergent difficulty is why two similar-looking games fight back in completely different ways, and the avatar that can tell them apart predicts a new game's danger instead of just reacting to it
evidence_needed: Devlog segments from Its Rascal, Zoteling and CodyCantEatThis building a hard section: do they place and tune specific obstacles, or adjust system values and watch what difficulty falls out?

question: Where does the maker's energy actually go across a year?
pole_low: starting; a trail of prototypes, each abandoned when it got hard or boring
pole_high: finishing; the current game ships even through the boring middle
why: The starter-versus-finisher split is the beginner's-eye question the whole lane exists to ask, and it is also a coaching curriculum: the avatar that can name which mode it is in can be nudged out of prototype-hopping and into shipping a run
evidence_needed: Channel-history samples from RookieDev, NathanOnDev and Barji: how many started projects per shipped or completed one, and do their own devlogs name the pattern?

question: When a game feels good to play, where does the feel mostly live: in the input response itself (instant, weighty, forgiving controls) or in the feedback dressing laid over it (sound, shake, particles, hitstop)?
pole_low: feel is in the controls themselves
pole_high: feel is manufactured by feedback effects
why: The avatar reading a new game should know what it is actually steering: if the feel is dressing, muting the presentation reveals the real handling, and its commentary should praise or blame the right layer
evidence_needed: Analyst segments from Jack Sather's game-feel essays and The Game Overanalyser separating control response from feedback effects on one specific game, with timestamps

question: How honest is a game's difficulty: does it challenge through readable threats the player could in principle have answered, or through hidden information, sudden spikes and punishment nobody could have seen coming?
pole_low: difficulty from unreadable or hidden punishment
pole_high: difficulty from readable threats, fairly telegraphed
why: The answer calibrates trust after a death: an honest game's deaths are information the avatar should analyse out loud, a dishonest game's deaths are noise it should name as unfair instead of apologising for
evidence_needed: Analyst segments from The Game Overanalyser's deep single-game analyses and Indie Game Clinic arguing the fairness of specific deaths or spikes, with timestamps

question: How does a game teach its systems: through explicit instruction (text, prompts, forced lessons) or through arrangement (levels that stage safe first encounters and let the player infer the rule)?
pole_low: taught by explicit instruction
pole_high: taught by designed first encounters
why: The avatar can mirror the game's own teaching when it coaches the kid: if the game teaches by arrangement, the avatar narrates the arrangement instead of reciting a manual the game never wrote
evidence_needed: Design-talk segments from Game Design Library and Jack Sather breaking down how one game introduces a mechanic without a tutorial screen, with timestamps

question: Where do a game's best moments come from: authored set pieces the designer scripted beat by beat, or systems colliding in ways nobody scripted?
pole_low: best moments are authored set pieces
pole_high: best moments are emergent system collisions
why: The answer tells the avatar where to hunt: authored games reward finding and performing the scripted beats, emergent games reward setting up collisions and getting out of the way
evidence_needed: Analyst segments from The Game Overanalyser and Tesseract attributing celebrated moments of a specific game to scripting versus systems, with timestamps

question: How much of a game's fun survives being watched rather than played: is the pleasure in the hands (execution and feel) or on the screen (readable state, visible stakes, legible cause and effect)?
pole_low: fun lives in the hands, dull to watch
pole_high: fun is fully legible to a watcher
why: Coach Player is a watched product: the avatar should grade a new game on watchability before committing a session to it, and lean its commentary toward whatever a watcher can actually see
evidence_needed: Analyst segments from Jack Sather and Game Design Library discussing spectator legibility of a specific game, checked against one performer video of the same game, with timestamps

question: How much does a game tell the player before a decision versus only after it: are outcomes previewable (ranges, previews, telegraphs, exact costs) or learnable only by paying for the lesson?
pole_low: learn only by paying for the lesson
pole_high: outcomes previewable before committing
why: The answer sets the avatar's talk: previewable games reward planning aloud and exact numbers, pay-to-learn games reward cheap experiments and treating early losses as tuition
evidence_needed: Analyst segments from The Game Overanalyser and Indie Game Clinic on information design in one game (previews, hidden odds, telegraphing), with timestamps

question: How concentrated is a game's fun: does it rest on one load-bearing trick (a single number, a timer, a scarcity, a physics edge) or is it spread across many systems that each contribute a little?
pole_low: fun spread thin across many systems
pole_high: one load-bearing trick carries the game
why: Finding the load-bearing trick first is the fastest way to read a new game: the avatar should test the trick early, and coach nudges should aim at it instead of at surface features
evidence_needed: Analyst segments from Jack Sather and Tesseract identifying the single mechanic or number a specific game's fun depends on, with timestamps

question: How visible is the designer's intent while playing: can the player feel what the game wants them to feel and do next, moment to moment, or does the intent only become clear in hindsight and analysis?
pole_low: designer intent opaque during play
pole_high: designer intent felt moment to moment
why: An avatar that can feel intent can perform the design instead of merely surviving it, and can tell the coach 'the game is pushing us toward the bridge' as a real read rather than a guess
evidence_needed: Analyst segments from The Game Overanalyser reconstructing designer intent for a specific sequence and showing where play reveals it, with timestamps

question: What does a game charge for failure, and how steep is the price: a slap (seconds lost, instant retry) or a real bill (progress, resources or a run)?
pole_low: failure is nearly free
pole_high: failure is expensive, progress is lost
why: The avatar's stake narration must match the game's real price list: invented dread over a free retry reads as lying, and shrugging at a lost run reads as not understanding what just happened
evidence_needed: Developer-facing segments from Indie Game Clinic and Game Design Library on failure cost and checkpoint design in specific games, with timestamps

question: When analysts find a flaw in a game, where do they locate the fix: in the numbers (tuning, costs, timings, drop rates) or in the structure (the rules and the information those numbers live inside)?
pole_low: the fix is in the numbers
pole_high: the fix is in the structure
why: This teaches two depths of diagnosis: the avatar's debriefs, and eventually the kid's own questions, should name which depth a proposed change lives at, because a numbers fix is a nudge and a structure fix is a redesign
evidence_needed: Advice segments from Indie Game Clinic and design talks in Game Design Library where a specific flaw is diagnosed and a fix proposed, with the depth of the fix identifiable, with timestamps

question: What is a game's posture toward its own unintended behaviour: are exploits, physics quirks and sequence breaks treated as errors to patch away, or kept and canonised as part of the game?
pole_low: unintended behaviour is patched away
pole_high: quirks are kept and become the game
why: The avatar must know whether breaking a system is playing it wrong or playing it best: in a canonising game the saboteur run is legitimate mastery, in a patching game it is a bug report with better jokes
evidence_needed: Analyst segments from Tesseract and The Game Overanalyser on kept bugs, exploits and patch history for a specific game, with timestamps

question: How does a game scale its challenge as it goes: by demanding more execution (faster, tighter, more precise) or by demanding more understanding (new combinations, deeper reads of the same systems)?
pole_low: challenge scales by execution demand
pole_high: challenge scales by understanding demand
why: The answer changes what practice means mid-run: execution games reward repetitions the coach can drill, understanding games reward scouting and talk before the next attempt
evidence_needed: Analyst segments from The Game Overanalyser and Game Design Library tracing how one game's late game differs from its early game, with timestamps

question: How does a game treat its quiet stretches: as dead time to be skipped or sped through, or as designed valleys (travel, tending, rebuilding, the trip back) that make the peaks land?
pole_low: quiet time is dead time to cut
pole_high: valleys are designed and load-bearing
why: The avatar's downtime behaviour should match the game's design: filling a designed valley with hype tramples it, while sitting silent through genuinely dead time abandons the audience
evidence_needed: Analyst segments from Jack Sather and Game Design Library on pacing and quiet stretches in a specific game, with timestamps

question: How readable are a game's rules from inside play: can a player infer the underlying numbers and rules from feedback alone, or do they need a wiki, data mining or patch notes to know what the game is doing?
pole_low: rules opaque without outside sources
pole_high: rules inferable from feedback alone
why: The avatar should narrate inferred rules with honest confidence levels and flag where the game hides them; for a clever middle-school audience, showing the inference is the curriculum, not just the conclusion
evidence_needed: Analyst segments from The Game Overanalyser and Tesseract reverse-engineering a specific game's hidden rules and showing which were inferable from play, with timestamps

question: Where does a game put its novelty across a run: in new mechanics drip-fed one by one, or in new combinations of a small fixed kit the player already knows?
pole_low: novelty from new mechanics arriving
pole_high: novelty from recombining a fixed kit
why: The answer shapes the avatar's session arc talk: drip-fed games promise 'wait for what unlocks next', recombination games promise 'wait for what we try next', and the coach should know which promise the game can keep
evidence_needed: Analyst segments from Jack Sather and Game Design Library on how one game sustains novelty across its length, with timestamps

question: When a teacher builds a new system, how much is designed as reusable architecture before any code, versus hacked together to work once?
pole_low: hack first, it just has to work
pole_high: architecture first, designed to be reused and extended
why: Architecture-first builders (Code Monkey's modular Unity systems) produce games the avatar can read and predict; hack-first builders ship faster but their games surprise even them. An avatar that knows which kind of builder made a game sets its expectations for how systems will behave at the edges
evidence_needed: Timestamped tutorial segments from Code Monkey and NOBL Games where a system is started from nothing, plus a DevWorm build started the opposite way, coded for design-before-code versus code-before-design.

question: What happens to prototype code once the idea proves fun: thrown away and rewritten clean, or kept and grown into the shipped game?
pole_low: prototype is sacred, ship the hack
pole_high: prototype is a sketch, rewrite it properly
why: The fate of the prototype is the deepest split in small-team building. Rewrite cultures produce readable, tunable games; keep-it cultures produce fast, weird, debt-heavy ones. It changes what an avatar can assume about how consistent a game's systems will feel hour to hour
evidence_needed: Devlog segments from Goodgis and NOBL Games revisiting early prototype code late in a project, and Code Monkey project-structure videos showing whether the tutorial prototype survives into the final build.

question: When a teacher tunes physics (jump height, gravity, slide, knockback), are the values derived from numbers and formulas worked out in advance, or found by playing and nudging until it feels right?
pole_low: pure feel, nudge until it feels right
pole_high: pure numbers, computed before testing
why: This is the maker version of the show lane's stake question: numbers-first physics feels consistent and readable to a player, feel-first physics feels alive and occasionally arbitrary. It decides whether the avatar should trust a game's physics as a system it can learn exactly, or as a mood it should surf
evidence_needed: Timestamped tuning segments from DevWorm (Godot 2D movement) and Code Monkey (character controller values) where a constant is chosen, coded for whether a calculation or a playtest came first.

question: How does the teacher build enemy behaviour: simple state machines with readable states, or layered systems whose behaviour emerges and can surprise the builder?
pole_low: simple readable state machines
pole_high: layered systems, behaviour emerges
why: Readable AI can be coached against: the avatar can name the state and predict the switch. Emergent AI produces the disasters and miracles the show lane lives on. Which one a game uses changes the avatar's whole risk posture moment to moment
evidence_needed: Enemy-AI tutorial segments from Code Monkey (state machine builds) and Farhan Aqeel (AI behaviour builds), coded for how much behaviour is explicitly scripted versus arising from interacting rules.

question: How is movement through the world solved: hand-placed waypoints and authored routes, or dynamic pathfinding the builder tunes and trusts?
pole_low: hand-authored routes and waypoints
pole_high: dynamic pathfinding, tuned and trusted
why: Authored routes make NPCs feel intentional and make a world legible; dynamic pathing makes crowds feel alive and occasionally very stupid in public. An avatar playing alongside NPCs reads encounters completely differently under each regime
evidence_needed: Pathfinding tutorial segments from Code Monkey (grid/A* builds) and DevWorm (Godot navigation) where a route system is chosen and its failure cases shown on screen.

question: When does performance get its say: is there a budget from day one (draw calls, pooling, profiling as a habit), or does optimisation arrive only when the game starts to hurt?
pole_low: optimise only when it hurts
pole_high: budget from day one, profile as you go
why: Budget-first builders ship games whose spectacle scales predictably; hurt-first builders ship games that fall over exactly at the biggest moments. The avatar's showmanship dial should behave differently in a game that will hold 60fps through the disaster and one that will not
evidence_needed: Optimisation and object-pooling segments from Code Monkey, plus NOBL Games studio-process videos where frame rate or build size forces a decision mid-project.

question: How much does the teacher invest in building their own tools (custom inspectors, level editors, debug overlays) versus working around what the engine gives them?
pole_low: engine defaults, work around them
pole_high: builds a tool for every recurring pain
why: Tool-builders compound: every project gets faster and their games carry a visible house style of debug views and editors. Engine-default builders stay portable and improvisational. It predicts how a maker's next game will differ from their last
evidence_needed: Custom-editor and tooling segments from Code Monkey (Unity editor tools) and Goodgis (process videos), coded for time spent building tools versus time spent using them.

question: While playing someone else's game, how much of the builder's running commentary is about how the game is probably BUILT (its state machines, its triggers, its reused systems) versus about what is happening in the fiction?
pole_low: plays immersed, fiction only
pole_high: constantly reverse-engineers the build
why: This is the Maker Lane's signature habit and the avatar's fastest route into a new game: a builder who narrates construction sees the staircase, the trigger volume and the recycled boss before they fire. It decides whether our avatar's commentary teaches the audience to see games, not just watch them
evidence_needed: Gameplay-with-commentary segments from Goodgis and DevWorm playing or reviewing games not their own, coded line by line for construction claims versus fiction claims, cross-checked against Code Monkey review-style videos.

question: Where do a game's values live in the teacher's builds: exposed as data (configs, spreadsheets, designer-facing objects anyone can retune) or buried in code where only the programmer can reach them?
pole_low: values buried in code
pole_high: everything exposed as tunable data
why: Data-driven games can be rebalanced live, modded, and read from the outside; code-buried games hide their tuning until behaviour leaks it. For a coach product this is the difference between a game the coach can retune between sessions and one they can only plead with
evidence_needed: Data-structure segments from Code Monkey (ScriptableObject-style architecture) and Farhan Aqeel, coded for where health, speed and damage numbers are shown living.

question: Inside one project, does the teacher build each feature as a bespoke one-off, or force features through generic reusable systems even when it costs more up front?
pole_low: bespoke one-offs per feature
pole_high: generic systems, features are configurations
why: Generic-system games feel coherent and break in families (one bug, everywhere); bespoke games feel hand-made and break one room at a time. The avatar's failure commentary and its predictions about where a game will glitch both depend on which kind it is inside
evidence_needed: Project-structure walkthroughs from NOBL Games and Code Monkey series builds, coded for how often an existing system is reused versus a new script written for one feature.

question: When a build breaks, what is the teacher's first move: patch the visible symptom and keep momentum, or stop and hunt the root cause in the architecture?
pole_low: patch the symptom, keep moving
pole_high: stop everything, find the root cause
why: Root-cause builders produce games that get more stable as they grow; symptom-patchers accumulate haunted corners everyone learns to avoid. It also models, for the kid audience, two honest ways to relate to your own mistakes, and the avatar will narrate its failures one way or the other
evidence_needed: Bug-fixing segments from DevWorm and Goodgis devlogs where a defect is found on camera, coded for time-to-patch versus time-to-diagnosis before the fix lands.

question: What gets built first in a new project: the smallest playable core loop, or the breadth of systems and content the loop will eventually sit inside?
pole_low: core loop first, smallest playable thing
pole_high: systems and content breadth first
why: Loop-first builders find the fun in week one and their games feel focused; breadth-first builders find their scope problems in month six and their games feel abundant. It is the clearest predictor of what a devlog series will look like at episode ten
evidence_needed: First-episode segments of multi-part series from NOBL Games, Goodgis and DevWorm, coded for what exists at the end of episode one: a playable loop or a shelf of systems.

question: When a new mechanic is born in a tutorial or devlog, which direction does it travel: from a player-feel goal backwards to the code, or from a neat technical trick forwards to whatever fun it happens to produce?
pole_low: tech trick first, fun discovered after
pole_high: player-feel goal first, code serves it
why: Feel-first mechanics read as intentional to players and teach well; trick-first mechanics produce the happy accidents whole channels are built on. The avatar meeting a new mechanic should be able to guess its origin, because origin predicts whether the mechanic will be fair
evidence_needed: Mechanic-introduction segments from Goodgis (design-forward builds) and Farhan Aqeel and DevWorm (feature builds), coded for whether a feel goal or a technique is stated first.

question: How small are the teacher's test increments while building: play the game after nearly every change, or build a whole feature and meet it all at once?
pole_low: whole feature, then test
pole_high: test after nearly every change
why: Tiny-increment builders catch misunderstandings while they are cheap and their on-camera failures are small and instructive; big-bang builders meet their features like opponents. It sets the rhythm of failure the audience learns to expect from making things
evidence_needed: Any full build session from Code Monkey and DevWorm, coded by counting editor-to-play transitions per finished feature.

question: Across projects, does the teacher carry a growing personal library of code and assets they reuse, or start each game as a fresh pile?
pole_low: fresh pile every project
pole_high: a personal library, carried and curated
why: Library builders accelerate visibly across a channel's history and their games rhyme; fresh-pile builders reinvent and occasionally leap. For Coach Player this is the builder's version of series memory, and it predicts how fast a maker's third game arrives compared to their first
evidence_needed: Cross-project comparisons from Code Monkey's long-running series and NOBL Games' catalogue videos, coded for reused controllers, UI kits and systems appearing across separate games.

question: When the avatar enters an unfamiliar game, how does it read the game's physics intent: faithful simulation it must respect, or exaggerated cartoon physics it can exploit
pole_low: reads physics as law, plays carefully inside it
pole_high: reads physics as a toy, probes for exploitable exaggeration
why: A physics-first avatar wastes its best moves in a cartoon game and dies stupidly in a simulation. Reading the intent early decides its whole risk posture. Axis drafted by MiniMax (fleet mining 2026-10-14), reframed by Muse toward avatar behaviour
evidence_needed: Maker and analyst transcripts where physics intent is discussed (Barji, Juniper Dev, Jack Sather), plus the avatar's own first-session logs once it plays

question: How visibly does a game teach its own rules in the first minutes, and how much must the avatar discover by experiment instead
pole_low: the game teaches explicitly, the avatar can trust instruction
pole_high: the game teaches nothing, every rule is an experiment
why: An avatar that experiments in a teaching game looks dumb; one that waits for instruction in a discovery game never moves. The detection changes its opening behaviour completely
evidence_needed: Design analyst transcripts on teaching without tutorials (Game Design Library, The Game Overanalyser) and maker devlogs on first-five-minutes design

question: How much failure information does the game itself hand back (explicit feedback, replays, stats) versus how much the avatar must reconstruct forensically
pole_low: the game explains every failure, the avatar just listens
pole_high: the game says nothing, the avatar must rebuild the cause itself
why: Decides whether the avatar's post-mortem move is a reading or an investigation, and how much of the debrief the coach can trust. Axis from MiniMax fleet mining, reframed by Muse
evidence_needed: Analyst transcripts on failure feedback design, plus Jesse Gillett style forensic segments as the high-pole behaviour model

question: How scarce is the game's core resource really, beneath its presentation: generous economy wearing a scarce costume, or true scarcity
pole_low: abundance in costume, the avatar can spend freely
pole_high: true scarcity, every spend is a commitment
why: Misreading scarcity is the classic new-player death. A maker-trained avatar audits drop rates and prices before it trusts the story the game tells about them
evidence_needed: Maker transcripts on economy design (Indie Game Clinic, CodyCantEatThis) and analyst economy breakdowns

question: How much of a game's experience is authored set pieces versus systems colliding, and where should the avatar expect the memorable moments to come from
pole_low: authored, the avatar plays the script well
pole_high: systemic, the avatar manufactures moments by colliding systems
why: The avatar performs differently in each world: precision in authored games, provocation in systemic ones. Pairs with spectacle-001 from the game side of the glass
evidence_needed: Design essays on emergence vs authorship (Jack Sather, Game Overanalyser), devlogs where a kept accident became the game (Juniper Dev, Zoteling)

question: How much difficulty control does the game hand the player (settings, assists, self-imposed rules), and should the avatar treat that as part of the game or as a coach-level decision
pole_low: difficulty is the game's, the avatar plays what is served
pole_high: difficulty is a player surface, the avatar and coach tune it openly
why: For a coached avatar this decides who owns challenge: the product's youngest users will reach for these levers, and the avatar needs a stance before they do. Axis from MiniMax fleet mining, reframed by Muse
evidence_needed: Analyst transcripts on accessibility and difficulty design (Indie Game Clinic), plus playtest evidence once the avatar has coach sessions

question: How confidently must the overseer believe an existing tile fits the situation before it runs the tile instead of escalating to the author
pole_low: escalates on any doubt, quality over cost, the library stays thin
pole_high: runs the closest tile almost always, cost over fit, the library stays small by force
why: This single threshold sets the whole system's economics: the LLM pulse rate, the budget burn, and how often play visibly stumbles. Stated by Casey 2026-10-14: the Jev must be able to say none of these are good enough
evidence_needed: Session logs once the tile runner exists: escalation rate vs session quality, plus Voyager's verification economics as the published baseline

question: When an interruption appears mid-plan, how much better than the A-plan must it score before the avatar bends toward it
pole_low: bends for any edge, lively but jittery, plans rarely complete
pole_high: bends only for a clear win, steady but misses quiet opportunities
why: Casey's trolling rule: you hope to be interrupted, but a text from a nearby boat does not make you beeline. The bend threshold is the avatar's opportunism dial and the coach will want to see it
evidence_needed: Session logs: interruptions offered vs taken vs regretted, coach overrides as the ground truth of a wrong threshold

question: When bending toward an interruption, how much should the route harvest value on the way (good water en route) versus arriving fast
pole_low: beeline, arrive fast, pass up everything between
pole_high: harvest route, slower arrival, value collected on the way compounds
why: Casey, 2026-10-14: you never just beeline to where the fish are reported; you cross the highest-probability water to get there. Decides pathing behaviour in every replan
evidence_needed: Replan logs: value collected en route vs arrival-time cost, across game types (open world vs level-based)

question: How short should the planning horizon get as a situation tightens, before the system asks the coach to grab the wheel
pole_low: stands down early, coach drives every tight spot personally
pole_high: keeps planning down to seconds, coach intervenes only on failure
why: The keyhole rule: first time through a tight passage with unknown wind and current, a responsible captain does not hand it to the autopilot. This question is the trust boundary of the whole product
evidence_needed: Coach takeover logs: which tight spots the coach chose to drive vs regretted delegating; near-miss reviews in debriefs

question: How large should a tile be: a single intention the coach can hold at once, or a chained routine that runs several intentions
pole_low: small tiles, coach assembles, overseer decides constantly
pole_high: large tiles, coach picks one and watches, overseer mostly idle
why: Granularity sets who thinks how often. Mindcraft's history is the evidence: parameterized commands won because they were the size of an intention, not an input and not a campaign
evidence_needed: Tile library statistics: reuse counts and failure rates by tile size; Mindcraft's command set as a worked example

question: When is a tile finished: when it works, or only when it passes the light-switch test and the coach forgets its mechanics entirely
pole_low: works is enough, graduation is a test pass
pole_high: invisible or unfinished, graduation requires the coach to use it for something else and never think about how
why: Casey's standard, 2026-10-14: the code has to be so good it goes invisible, like wiring behind a light switch. This question decides whether the library fills with tools or with appliances
evidence_needed: Graduation reviews in the workshop: tiles the coach had to ask about vs tiles never thought about again; explanation requests counted per tile

question: How strongly should a projected mechanic from creator transcripts be believed before it becomes a tile, given narration can exaggerate what the hands actually did
pole_low: only mechanics visible in outcomes count, narration is advertising
pole_high: narration counts as testimony, most stated mechanics become tiles pending disproof
why: The whole Codex-to-tiles pipeline stands on this: we project lower mechanics out of talk. Too strict and the library starves; too loose and it fills with theatre moves that never existed
evidence_needed: Projection audits: tiles built from transcripts, then tested in play — success rate by how the mechanic was evidenced (stated, shown in outcomes, or both)

question: While a tile runs, how patient should the overseer be with its slow start before judging it the wrong tile
pole_low: judges in seconds, wrong tiles die fast, right tiles sometimes die young
pole_high: judges on the tile's own timescale, slow starters get their full run
why: Every scripted behaviour has a wind-up (a troll pass needs the full pass). Impatient overseers thrash; patient ones ride disasters to the bottom. Pairs with the failure-dwell evidence from the Coach lane
evidence_needed: Tile abort logs vs outcomes had the tile finished; the format-change rule applied to aborts (was it the tile, or the situation)

question: How much of the question graph should ride into an authoring call when the LLM writes a new script
pole_low: only the questions about this exact situation, a narrow beam
pole_high: the whole relevant frontier: the situation, the game, the avatar's character, hundreds of shaded questions
why: Casey, 2026-10-14: the questioning projects into the call so the LLM starts from a vast array of how to make it better, not a blank prompt. Beam width trades focus against the accidents where distant questions turn out to be the point
evidence_needed: Authoring event logs: which priming questions the resulting script actually used, judged at verification and in later reuse

question: When the library holds several tiles that all fit, should the overseer pick the most proven, or rotate toward the least-tested that still clears the bar
pole_low: most proven always, sessions are reliable and a little samey
pole_high: rotate deliberately, sessions vary and the library learns from use
why: This is the exploration dial of the whole system, and it is where personality leaks in: two avatars with the same library play differently by this question alone
evidence_needed: Library health reports: usage concentration vs character distinctness in debriefs; whether rotation discoveries graduate or get pruned
